title: Variables and types
summary: Give values a name, and learn why every value in C# has a type.

steps.title: A variable is a named box
body: A **variable** stores a value so you can use it later. In C# you say what *kind* of value the box holds, then its name, then the value.
`int` and `string` are **types**. `int` holds whole numbers, `string` holds text. The `=` sign means *store the value on the right in the variable on the left*. It is not a question about equality.

steps.prompt: Declare a whole-number variable called `score` holding `100`.
steps.explain: Type first, then the name, then `=` and the value.

steps.title: The everyday types
body: The type is a promise. The compiler holds you to it, which is how it catches mistakes *before* the program runs:
int count = "five";   // error: a string is not an int

steps.prompt: Match each type to a value it can hold.
Will the compiler accept each line?
steps.explain: Double quotes make a `string`, single quotes make exactly one `char`. A whole number fits in a `double` (it becomes `2.0`), but text never fits in a number.

steps.title: Changing a variable, and var
body: A variable can be given a new value. You only write the type the first time.
lives = 2;            // no 'int' here: the box already exists
`var` asks the compiler to work the type out from the value. The variable is still strongly typed. It just saves typing.
var city = "Nairobi";   // the compiler sees a string
> **Tip:** Names use *camelCase* by convention: `firstName`, `totalPrice`. They cannot start with a digit or contain spaces.

steps.explain: `int y = x;` copies the value `5` into `y`. Changing `x` afterwards does not touch `y`.
`var` is not a type. It tells the compiler to infer one, and a number with a decimal point is a `double`.

steps.title: Fix the types
prompt: Each variable has the wrong type for its value. Fix the **types** (not the values) so the program compiles and prints:
hints: Text in double quotes is a `string`. A whole number is an `int`.
A number with a decimal point is a `double`, and `true`/`false` is a `bool`.

steps.title: Swap two variables
prompt: `a` and `b` hold the wrong values. Swap them **without retyping the numbers**, so the program prints:
You will need a third variable to hold one value while you overwrite it.

require.message: Keeps the two starting lines unchanged

forbid.message: Swaps using the variables, not by retyping 1 and 2

hints: If you write `a = b;` first, the old value of `a` is lost. Save it somewhere before that.
`int temp = a;` then `a = b;` then `b = temp;`

steps.title: Your code inside Sidekick
body: From now on, the last exercise of each lesson is a **piece of Sidekick**. Your code runs inside a small method
the dojo wraps around it. Some variables are **given** (already declared and filled in), and you leave your answer
// Given: string name = "Ada"; int goalMinutes = 360;   and   string result = "";
Do not declare `name` or `result` again: they already exist, so `string result = ...` would be an error. Just
`$"..."` is an **interpolated string**: every `{ }` inside it is replaced by the value of what is in the braces.
You will study it properly in *Strings*; for now `$"{name} has {count} tasks"` is all you need.

steps.title: Your daily goal line
prompt: **Sidekick piece: the goal line `sk` prints under your greeting.** Your code becomes the body of
`static string ProfileLine(string name, int goalMinutes, int loggedMinutes)`: `name`, `goalMinutes` and
`loggedMinutes` are given. Put the line in `result`:
<name>: <logged> min logged, <remaining> min to go (goal <goal> min)
| `Ada` | `360` | `90` | `Ada: 90 min logged, 270 min to go (goal 360 min)` |
| `Linus` | `300` | `300` | `Linus: 300 min logged, 0 min to go (goal 300 min)` |
Use at least one variable of your own (the remaining minutes are a good one) and keep the word `min` in a
`string` variable so it is typed once.
starter: // name, goalMinutes and loggedMinutes are given. Put the line in result.
template: static string ProfileLine(string name, int goalMinutes, int loggedMinutes)
Dojo.Eq("Ada, 90 of 360", "Ada: 90 min logged, 270 min to go (goal 360 min)", ProfileLine("Ada", 360, 90));
Dojo.Eq("Linus, goal reached exactly", "Linus: 300 min logged, 0 min to go (goal 300 min)", ProfileLine("Linus", 300, 300));
Dojo.Eq("nothing logged yet", "Grace: 0 min logged, 480 min to go (goal 480 min)", ProfileLine("Grace", 480, 0));
Dojo.Eq("a short goal", "Sam: 15 min logged, 15 min to go (goal 30 min)", ProfileLine("Sam", 30, 15));
hints: `result = $"{name}: {loggedMinutes} min logged, {remaining} min to go (goal {goalMinutes} min)";` gives the shape; now move `min` into a `string` variable.
steps.explain: Sidekick calls your `ProfileLine` with your real name and today's logged minutes every time you open it.

build.title: Your daily goal line
build.unlocks: `sk` now shows how far you are from today's goal.
transform: // Your daily goal line: your own passing code from the code-dojo C# track (First steps > Variables and types).
static string ProfileLine(string name, int goalMinutes, int loggedMinutes)
